newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Prospect of Cyprus talks improving, says UN envoy.
newsitem.headline: Prospect of Cyprus talks improving, says UN envoy.

text.p: Prospects are improving for the resumption of direct talks between Greek and Turkish Cypriots by June, the U.N. envoy in divided Cyprus said on Friday.
"I think we are getting closer," said Gustave Feissel, resident representative of the U.N. secretary-general in Cyprus.

"Of course until we get there...it doesn't matter if you are 95 percent near the goal, you have to be 100 percent and that is what we are trying to achieve," he added after meeting President Glafcos Clerides, the Greek Cypriot leader.

Amid growing tension and fears of a military buildup, international pressure has been mounting for a solution to the decades-old Cyprus problem ahead of the possible start of talks on its joining the European Union.
International mediators are looking to June for the first meeting in almost three years between Clerides and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash.

U.N. special envoy Han Sung-joo, a former foreign minister of South Korea, arrives on the island on Saturday. He is due to participate in separate meetings together with Feissel with the two leaders next week.

A U.N. peacekeeping force has been stationed in Cyprus since 1963. The island has been divided since Turkey invaded its northern third in 1974 after a coup sponsored by Athens. A small army of mediators has failed for decades to reunite it under a federal umbrella.

The United Nations has been working on the adoption of goodwill gestures by both sides to improve the climate for talks, soured after the killings of three Greek Cypriots on the ceasefire line by Turks or Turkish Cypriots and the shooting of a Turkish Cypriot sentry last year.

Clerides is president of the administration in the south, internationally recognised as the island's only legitimate government. Denktash heads a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in the north recognised only by Ankara.
The 1,200-strong U.N. force patrols a buffer zone between some 30,000 mainland Turkish forces in northern Cyprus and 11,500 Greek Cypriot conscripts in the south.
